st.headline: DeepSeek set to raise at least $15 billion in Tencent-backed funding
st.teaser: Tencent Holdings has committed among the largest amounts in the current financing, sources said.
fullText: DeepSeek is close to securing at least 80 billion yuan (S$15 billion) in its latest round of funding, blowing past its own capital-raising target ahead of a landmark initial public offering in early 2027 .

Battery pioneer Contemporary Amperex Technology and WeChat-operator Tencent Holdings have committed among the largest amounts in the current financing, which closes soon, sources familiar with the matter said.

DeepSeek initially sought about 50 billion yuan, but interest outstripped expectations after the successful release of its latest AI model, the sources said, asking not to be named as the details are not public.
Based on term sheets signed, the final tally could approach 100 billion yuan, they added.
DeepSeek’s funding sets the stage for one of the most highly anticipated Chinese market debuts in years.
The company is riding high after the release of the V4 Flash large language model, which reset expectations for cost versus performance against leaders Anthropic and OpenAI.

That caps a strong run for founder Liang Wenfeng , whose start-up has forged a reputation for technical breakthroughs since a 2025 model that matched the capabilities of Silicon Valley offerings at a fraction of the cost.
As with other artificial intelligence players, DeepSeek requires huge amounts of capital to bankroll its ambitions in a potentially revolutionary technology.

The company plans to deploy at least 160,000 of Huawei Technologies’ top accelerators at a massive data centre it is building in Inner Mongolia, which may create one of the largest known clusters of Huawei AI chips.
It has publicly released software created with Huawei to program AI chips, a foray into a new arena in close partnership with the hardware leader .
Rival Moonshot, meanwhile, is also targeting an early 2027 IPO after closing funding at a US$50 billion (S$64 billion) valuation.
Liang pledged in at least one meeting with investors in 2026 that he will keep developing open AI models while pursuing a broader goal of achieving artificial general intelligence.
The hedge fund manager made it clear his main goal was to push the boundaries of the technology rather than monetisation, Bloomberg News has reported.
While discussions around the current deal are near an end, details may still change in final talks, the sources said.
DeepSeek had originally targeted a valuation of about 500 billion yuan in its financing.
A CATL representative declined to comment, while Tencent had no immediate comment.
DeepSeek did not respond to an e-mailed request for comment during a Chinese public holiday.
DeepSeek has drawn enormous interest from would-be investors because it is one of a clutch of companies that sit at the heart of China’s effort to compete globally on AI.
Once the round closes, the next step should be to restructure the company to prepare for an IPO, the sources said.
Tencent, which also landed the biggest investment in the start-up at 10 billion yuan in a previous round of financing, aims to integrate AI into its platforms.
CATL may be eyeing an increasingly lucrative business of supplying components to the industry, including for data centres.

The AI lab’s capital-raising had attracted its share of controversy. DeepSeek briefly suspended the deal after comments widely attributed to Liang about US-Chinese AI competition went viral on social media.
Chinese media outlet Yicai reported in July that the billionaire entrepreneur had talked about a reliance on Nvidia chips and China’s persistent lag in AI sophistication relative to the US.
Liang’s net worth more than doubled to around US$36 billion when DeepSeek closed its first round of external fund-raising this summer.
The AI start-up grew as an offshoot from his hedge fund High-Flyer, which provided much of the initial support.
Liang contributed again in the previous 50 billion yuan round, which valued DeepSeek at roughly 350 billion yuan at the time. BLOOMBERG

cna.headline: Yemen's Houthis say they struck Riyadh airport, other Saudi sites
cna.teaser: A Houthi spokesman says the group had hit King Khalid International Airport, a refinery belonging to state oil giant Aramco and other targets in the kingdom's south.
fullText: TAIZ: Iran-backed Houthis said on Monday (Oct 6) they had struck Riyadh's international airport, an oil refinery and other sites in Saudi Arabia, as the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said they had destroyed Houthi targets on the Red Sea coast.

Pakistan and Türkiye have pledged to deploy troops to Saudi Arabia under a new mutual defence pact following weeks of Houthi attacks, as Riyadh and its Yemeni government allies began an ambitious push aimed at retaking all territory held by the group.

The fighting in Yemen has become the most active front in the Middle East war in recent weeks, displacing more than 184,000 people, the United Nations says, and deepening the conflict that has engulfed the wider region.

The Houthis previously controlled much of northern Yemen, including the capital Sanaa and the western city of Hodeida, but seized swathes of coastline last month along the Red Sea and key Bab el-Mandeb Strait, in Yemen's deadliest fighting in years.

The Yemeni military said it carried out more than 1,000 strikes and began an offensive against Sanaa, while the Saudi-led coalition supporting the internationally recognised government said 100 warplanes flew sorties at dawn.
Turki Al-Malki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition, said on X that its naval forces had hit "military targets" belonging to the Houthis in Hodeida on the Red Sea coast.
They "destroyed weapons depots, facilities storing booby-trapped boats and naval mines" and had "thwarted a planned attack" targeting waterways in the southern Red Sea, he said.

Later, the military said it had driven the Houthis from the area surrounding the Bab el-Mandeb Strait - a vital route for maritime traffic - including the port city of Mocha, Dhubab airport and Al-Omari military camp.
They also said they expelled the Houthis from several areas in Taiz in the southwest, where deadly fighting has surged in recent days.
Military sources stopped short of confirming an official announcement of Mocha's recapture, saying that pro-government forces had cut off the only supply route to the port.

Loud explosions rattled the Saudi capital on Monday evening, with a Houthi spokesman saying the group had hit King Khalid International Airport, a refinery belonging to state oil giant Aramco and other targets in the kingdom's south.
It came a day after Yemen's government announced the lofty goal of retaking all Houthi territory - home to most of the country's population, and much of it held for more than a decade.

Representatives of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye held an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Monday under the auspices of a joint defence agreement signed in August committing them to come to each other's aid in the event of any attack.
They also agreed "to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the Kingdom".
The statement did not specify what role the troops would fill once in Saudi Arabia.
A spokesman for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was "deeply concerned by the sharp escalation in fighting", and condemned "the continued Houthi cross-border attacks" on Saudi Arabia.
Houthi attacks have repeatedly targeted Saudi oil infrastructure, as well as its tankers in the Red Sea.

A source in the Saudi energy sector told AFP that an attack Sunday had again halted pumping by the East-West pipeline to the Red Sea, a key conduit for the kingdom's exports since Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz at the start of the wider Middle East war.
Crude prices had already been soaring as a result of the Middle East war before the Houthis began targeting the world's largest oil exporter.
Saudi Aramco chief executive Amin Nasser warned on Monday that global oil stockpiles were "scarily thin" owing to the war.
"The system is already straining," Nasser told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London.
